title: How to Teach Leadership Skills to Children
metaDescription: Teach leadership as behaviour - listening, fair decisions and shared responsibility - rather than confidence, volume or who talks the most.

sections.heading: Leadership is a set of behaviours, not a personality type
paragraphs: It's easy to assume the most confident child in the group, the one who speaks first and loudest, is automatically the "natural leader." That assumption causes real harm: it quietly tells quieter, slower-to-speak, or non-speaking children that leadership isn't for them, when in fact none of those traits are what actually makes a group work well together.

This guide treats leadership as a specific set of observable behaviours that any child can practise and improve at: listening carefully enough to summarise someone else's point, helping a group choose fairly between options, taking responsibility for a shared outcome rather than just their own part, and responding to a mistake without needing to blame someone for it. All four can be taught, practised, and noticed - which is exactly why they're a better classroom and family focus than something as vague as "confidence."

This article focuses on leadership as everyday group behaviour. If you're also working on how children generate and test their own ideas - spotting a problem and building something cheap to try it out - our companion guide on developing entrepreneurial thinking in children covers that earlier stage in more depth.

sections.heading: What to ignore (and what to look for instead)
paragraphs: Before running any of the activities below, it's worth being explicit about what doesn't count as evidence of leadership ability, because these are the easiest things to notice by accident. Don't score a child's confidence, how loudly or quickly they speak, or how much eye contact they make as signs of leadership - none of these reliably predict whether a group actually makes good, fair decisions together, and treating them as if they do disadvantages children who communicate differently.

Look instead for whether a child invites other people to contribute, shares responsibility for the outcome rather than claiming all the credit (or none of the blame), explains the reasoning behind a choice, and changes their approach in response to feedback. These are things you can actually see happen, regardless of how a child talks, moves, or communicates.

sections.heading: Give everyone a meaningful role
paragraphs: In any small group project, rotate clear roles - organiser, question-asker, materials checker, presenter - so every child gets practice at more than one kind of contribution over time. Make space for non-speaking or AAC (augmentative and alternative communication) based participation in every role, not just a token "quiet" one; a materials checker can tick off a picture list just as effectively by pointing as by talking.

Be explicit with the group about what a role actually means: a leader for the week is responsible for helping the group make progress, not entitled to tell everyone else what to do. That distinction - responsibility to the group, rather than authority over it - is worth repeating out loud more than once, because children (and plenty of adults) default to the opposite assumption.

sections.heading: Practise listening and disagreement
paragraphs: Give the group a small, fictional disagreement to work through - for example, deciding how to spend a pretend £10 activity budget between two things the group wants (this is a UK-style example in pounds; any small amount in any currency works just as well). Before anyone proposes a decision, ask each child to summarise someone else's view in their own words first. That single step - restating what you heard before you respond - does most of the work of teaching real listening.

Model respectful disagreement yourself: it's entirely possible to say "I don't think that's the best option, and here's why" without raising your voice or dismissing the other person. Actively invite quieter group members to contribute, but without putting them under pressure to speak if that's not how they communicate best - a written note, a drawn preference, or a simple point at a picture works just as well as a spoken opinion.

sections.heading: Make decisions transparently
paragraphs: Ask the group to agree on their decision-making criteria before comparing options - cost, fairness and safety are a reliable starting set for most children's activities. Once criteria are agreed, compare the options against them openly, out loud or in writing, rather than letting one person simply announce a choice.

If the plan changes partway through, say why, in front of the whole group, rather than quietly adjusting it. This single habit - explaining changes rather than just making them - turns leadership from something that happens inside one child's head into something the whole group can see and learn from.

sections.heading: Respond to mistakes without assigning blame
paragraphs: Mistakes are where leadership behaviour is tested most directly, so it's worth practising on purpose rather than only reacting to real ones as they happen. Use a scenario where a group runs out of materials partway through a project - for example, a group making a shared poster that runs short of card halfway through. Ask three questions: What happened? What can we repair right now? How do we prevent this next time?

Deliberately avoid letting the group settle on blaming one child for a shared shortfall - in almost every case, several small decisions led to the gap, and finding one person to blame teaches children to look for a scapegoat rather than to problem-solve together. Research on metacognition and self-regulation from the Education Endowment Foundation suggests that prompting children to reflect on what happened and what they'd do differently next time - rather than simply moving on - helps that kind of reasoning transfer to future situations, which is exactly the habit this exercise is meant to build.

sections.heading: Worked example: the poster that ran out of card
paragraphs: A group of four children is making a shared poster for a class display. Halfway through, they realise they've used more card than planned and won't have enough to finish the second half as designed. Rather than an adult stepping in to solve it, the group is asked to work through it themselves: what happened (too much was used on the first half before anyone checked how much was left), what can be repaired now (redesign the second half with a smaller layout, or use the back of an already-used sheet), and how to prevent it next time (check the materials halfway through, not just at the start).
The adult's role here is to ask the three questions and then stay quiet while the group works it out - resisting the urge to supply the fix is often harder for the adult than for the children.

sections.heading: Facilitator's step-by-step plan
list: Rotate roles at the start of each session, and agree what each role is actually responsible for.
Introduce the day's scenario and ask the group to agree their decision-making criteria before discussing options.
Ask each child to restate someone else's point before responding to it.
Compare the options against the agreed criteria openly, and have the group explain their choice out loud or in writing.
If something goes wrong, run the "what happened, what can we repair, how do we prevent it" sequence before moving on.

sections.heading: Making this accessible to every child
paragraphs: Every activity in this guide should flex to different communication styles and needs. For a child who uses AAC or doesn't use spoken language, build their contributions into the structure from the start rather than adding them as an afterthought - a role like "materials checker" or "criteria reminder" can be carried out entirely through pointing, a picture-based communication board, or a written list, with no speaking required at all.

For a child who finds group discussion overwhelming - too many voices, too much noise, too much eye contact expected of them - offer a smaller sub-group of two or three for the listening and disagreement practice, and allow extra processing time before expecting a response; several seconds of silence after a question is not a sign that a child doesn't understand, it's often exactly what they need to form an answer. A child can show they've understood a decision by pointing to the option they'd choose on a written or picture-based list, rather than explaining it verbally - that's an equally valid demonstration of the same thinking.

sections.heading: How to check understanding
paragraphs: The clearest sign a child has understood this isn't how confidently they talk about the activity afterwards - it's whether they can point to a specific decision and explain, in their own way, why the group chose it. Ask: "What did the group decide, and what was the reason?" and "What would you do differently next time, and why?"

A child who can answer both, even briefly or non-verbally, has grasped the behaviour this guide is trying to build. A child who can only say "we made a poster" or "I was in charge" without being able to connect that to a reason or a reflection has learned the activity's surface, not its point - which is a useful thing to notice and revisit, not a reason to worry.

sections.heading: Common teaching mistake to avoid
paragraphs: The mistake to watch for is rewarding the loudest, fastest, or most confident-sounding child by default, because it's the easiest signal to notice in a busy classroom or living room. Over time, that quietly teaches every child in the group - including the confident one - that leadership is about dominating a conversation rather than making it work well for everyone in it. Noticing and naming the quieter behaviours (summarising someone else's point, changing a plan based on feedback, sharing credit) takes more deliberate effort, but it's what actually builds the skill this guide is about.

sections.heading: Try this next
paragraphs: Pick one activity from this guide and repeat it with a different fictional scenario - choosing a game for a rainy afternoon, deciding how to arrange a shared shelf, or planning a small group task. Ask the child to explain one decision, using whichever method suits them best: spoken words, pictures, writing, or pointing. Keep any real family financial details out of the exercise; fictional numbers teach exactly the same lesson.

sections.heading: Editorial references
paragraphs: The approach to mistakes in this guide ("what happened, what can we repair, how do we prevent it") draws on the general principle behind the Education Endowment Foundation's guidance on metacognition and self-regulation, which supports structured reflection - planning, monitoring and evaluating one's own actions - as a way of helping children apply reasoning to future situations: https://educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/metacognition-and-self-regulation.

faqs.question: What age can children start practising these leadership behaviours?
faqs.answer: Even young children can practise a simplified version - taking turns, naming how a choice was made, saying what they'd do differently - from around age six or seven. The underlying behaviours stay the same; what changes with age is how much they can explain their own reasoning in words.

faqs.question: What if one child always wants to take charge?
faqs.answer: Rotating roles with a clear, stated job description for each one usually helps more than directly telling an eager child to step back. Frame it as "this week you're the question-asker, and the organiser role is someone else's job" rather than as a criticism of their enthusiasm.

faqs.question: My child is quiet and rarely speaks up in group activities. Does that mean they can't be a leader?
faqs.answer: No. Quietness and leadership ability are unrelated. Many of the behaviours this guide focuses on - listening carefully, noticing when a plan needs to change, treating a decision fairly - don't require speaking first or loudest, and a quiet child often does them very well once a role makes space for their preferred way of contributing.
